blocks.orig: Tanzania – the land of a savannah full of lions, zebras and giraffes. But also endless white beaches on the coast and on the islands. A developing country, which means that not everything is working the way we are used to. Below are some facts and tips that help you to be well prepared for your trip!
blocks.html: Tanzania – a country of savannah where lions, zebras and giraffes roam, yet also one of long white beaches along the coast and on its islands. It is a developing nation, so not everything runs the way you may be used to at home. The facts and tips below should help you arrive well prepared for your trip!

blocks.orig: Tanzania is located in East Africa between the Indian Ocean and neighboring countries Kenya, Mozambique, Congo, Malawi and Rwanda. The population is 58 million people who belong to more than 120 different tribes. Dar es Salaam on the coast is the largest city with 2.6 million inhabitants. The official capital of Tanzania is the much smaller Dodoma, which is located in the centre of the country. More than 120 different tribes live in Tanzania and more than 100 languages ​​are spoken in total. The largest tribes are the Sukuma, Nyamwezi, Haya, Nyakyusa and Chaggastam, each with more than a million members. However, there is no tribe that dominates, which contributes to the stable political climate.
blocks.html: Tanzania lies in East Africa, between the Indian Ocean and its neighbours Kenya, Mozambique, Congo, Malawi and Rwanda. Its 58 million inhabitants belong to more than 120 different tribes. The largest city is Dar es Salaam on the coast, home to 2.6 million people. The official capital, however, is the far smaller Dodoma in the centre of the country. Over 120 tribes live in Tanzania and together they speak more than 100 languages. The biggest groups are the Sukuma, Nyamwezi, Haya, Nyakyusa and Chaggastam, each numbering over a million members. No single tribe dominates, though, and that helps keep the political climate stable.

blocks.orig: Tanzania has two official languages: English and Kiswahili. In addition, many tribes have their own mother tongue. Kiswahili is not only spoken in Tanzania, but also (partially) in Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Mozambique and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Kiswahili originates from Bantu, but also uses some English and Arabic words. In Tanzania, most people speak mainly Kiswahili, often their mother tongue and sometimes English.
blocks.html: There are two official languages in Tanzania: English and Kiswahili. On top of that, many tribes speak their own mother tongue. Kiswahili is spoken not just in Tanzania but also (in part) in Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Mozambique and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The language has Bantu roots, with a number of English and Arabic words mixed in. Most Tanzanians speak Kiswahili above all, frequently their mother tongue too, and sometimes English.

blocks.orig: The term safari is Kiswahili and literally means travel. In the western world, however, we mainly associate a safari in Africa with observation of wild animals. The most popular animals are the Big Five: lions, elephants, buffaloes, leopards and rhinos. But Tanzania also has countless other impressive animal species and hundreds of beautiful, colorful birds. You can see them all with Your Tanzania Trip! Your private guide will be happy to tell you all about the animals, birds and plants you encounter along the way. During the safari you will use a 4 × 4 Landcruiser Jeep with a foldable roof from Your Tanzania Trip. Your Tanzania Trip only organizes private safaris, which means you don’t have to share the car with anyone. You decide when the safari starts and ends. In consultation with your guide, you can decide the schedule for the day. For example, if you suddenly feel like ending the day at the pool, that’s no problem. With a little luck you can even spot some wild animals from there.
blocks.html: The word safari comes from Kiswahili and simply means travel. In the western world, though, an African safari is mostly linked to watching wild animals. The animals people want to see most are the Big Five: lions, elephants, buffaloes, leopards and rhinos. Yet Tanzania is home to countless other remarkable species as well as hundreds of beautiful, colourful birds. With Your Tanzania Trip you can see them all! Your private guide will gladly explain everything about the animals, birds and plants you come across on the way. For the safari itself you travel in a Your Tanzania Trip 4 × 4 Landcruiser Jeep with a fold-up roof. Because Your Tanzania Trip only runs private safaris, you don’t have to share the vehicle with anyone else. You choose when the safari begins and ends, and together with your guide you set the programme for the day. Should you suddenly fancy finishing the day by the pool, that’s perfectly fine. With a bit of luck you might even spot wild animals from there.

blocks.orig: During the safari in Tanzania it is possible to visit a traditional tribe. The most famous tribe in Tanzania is probably the Maasai tribe. These are nomadic people who live off their cattle. The Maasai are known for their beautiful pearl jewelry, long spears in their hand and red shukkas (blankets that they wear as clothing). They live in semi-permanent huts – called manyattas – that are made of grass and dung. Traditional dance consists of jumping as high as possible. The oldest tribe in Tanzania, the Hadzabe, live around Lake Eyasi. Until recently they lived very isolated, but nowadays they accept to be visited by tourists. The Hadzabe still have a traditional lifestyle, which means that they mainly live from hunting. And just like the more southern San and Xhosa, they communicate in a click language.
blocks.html: While on safari in Tanzania you can also pay a visit to a traditional tribe. The best-known tribe in the country is probably the Maasai, nomadic people who make their living from their cattle. They are recognised by their beautiful pearl jewellery, the long spears they carry and their red shukkas (blankets worn as clothing). Their semi-permanent huts – known as manyattas – are built from grass and dung. In their traditional dance, the aim is to jump as high as you can. The oldest tribe in Tanzania, the Hadzabe, lives around Lake Eyasi. Until recently they kept very much to themselves, but today they are willing to receive tourists. The Hadzabe still follow a traditional way of life and mainly live from hunting. Like the San and Xhosa further south, they speak a click language.

blocks.orig: It is good to know that the animals are most active at sunrise and sunset. Then the temperatures in Tanzania are pleasant and animals are looking for food. The chance to see the animals in action is best during that time. But in the middle of the day there is still plenty of wildlife to see.
blocks.html: Worth knowing: animals are at their most active around sunrise and sunset. At those hours the temperatures in Tanzania are pleasant and the animals go out in search of food, so your chance of seeing them in action is greatest then. That said, there is still plenty of wildlife to be seen in the middle of the day.

blocks.orig: When traveling to Tanzania it is good to know what to expect. Below is the most useful useful travel information.
blocks.html: Before you travel to Tanzania it helps to know what lies ahead. Here you will find the most useful travel information.

blocks.orig: To enter Tanzania, you need a visa and a passport that is valid for at least six months upon return. You can apply for a visa in advance at the Tanzanian embassy in London/ Washington and costs 40 British pounds/ 50 US Dollar. It is also possible to request it upon arrival at the airport. In this case it costs 50 US dollars. If so, have a pen and $ 50 in cash ready. The waiting time is about an hour. Anyone traveling to Tanzania by land should best arrange the visa in advance to avoid long waiting times at the border.
blocks.html: For entry into Tanzania you need a visa and a passport that remains valid for at least six months after your return. The visa can be arranged beforehand at the Tanzanian embassy in London/ Washington, where it costs 40 British pounds/ 50 US Dollar. Alternatively you can apply on arrival at the airport, in which case the fee is 50 US dollars. If you choose that route, keep a pen and $ 50 in cash to hand. Expect to wait about an hour. If you are entering Tanzania overland, it is wise to sort out the visa in advance so you avoid long queues at the border.

blocks.orig: It is good to check with the embassy before traveling to see if the above rules are still valid!
blocks.html: Do check with the embassy before you leave whether the rules above still apply!

blocks.orig: The climate in Tanzania is characterized by two different seasons, which hardly differ from each other. The temperatures are pleasant throughout, but they can vary due to differences in altitude. Temperatures in the highlands are usually cooler, with a significant difference between day and night temperatures, while the coast is always warm and humid. During the day the temperature can reach 35°C /95°F.
blocks.html: Tanzania has a climate with two seasons, and the difference between them is small. Temperatures are pleasant year-round, although they vary with altitude. In the highlands it is generally cooler, with a marked gap between day and night temperatures, whereas the coast stays warm and humid at all times. Daytime temperatures can climb to 35°C /95°F.

blocks.orig: Tanzania has two rainy seasons. The short rainy season lasts from mid-October to the end of November and the long rainy season from the end of March to the end of May. However, during this time you can also go on a trip to Tanzania. Most of the roads are passable, the parks are lush and green and there are fewer tourists. The rain usually falls in the afternoon while the mornings are sunny. There is a chance that dirt roads in the parks become impassable due to heavy rain. In this case we are always looking for an alternative route!
blocks.html: There are two rainy seasons in Tanzania: the short rains from mid-October until the end of November, and the long rains from the end of March until the end of May. You can still travel to Tanzania during these months. Most roads remain passable, the parks are green and lush, and there are fewer visitors. Rain tends to fall in the afternoon, while the mornings are sunny. Heavy rain can occasionally make dirt roads in the parks impassable; when that happens we always look for another route!

blocks.orig: Tanzania is a safe destination for a vacation. It has even been named the safest country in Africa! The country is politically stable. Nevertheless, there is still a relatively high level of poverty in the country. It is therefore advisable to follow a number of rules. However, if you heed the following advice, which actually applies in every major European city, you are safe:
blocks.html: Tanzania is a safe country for a holiday and has even been named the safest country in Africa! Politically it is stable. Even so, poverty remains relatively widespread, so it makes sense to observe a few rules. If you stick to the advice below, which really applies in any large European city too, you will be safe:

blocks.orig: Never leave your passport, money or valuables open in the room
blocks.html: Never leave your passport, money or valuables lying around in your room

blocks.orig: Put your valuables in a locker or hand them in at the reception, where they will be kept in special lockers
blocks.html: Store valuables in a safe or hand them in at reception, where they are kept in dedicated lockers

blocks.orig: Do not leave important items (such as money or your bag) unattended in the safari vehicle, even for a short time
blocks.html: Never leave important items (money, your bag) unattended in the safari vehicle, not even briefly

blocks.orig: Leave precious jewelry at home. You can wear a (simple) necklace, watch, or wedding ring, but avoid flashy jewelry
blocks.html: Leave expensive jewellery at home. A (simple) necklace, watch or wedding ring is fine, but avoid anything flashy

blocks.orig: Don’t go out on the streets in the dark
blocks.html: Don’t walk the streets after dark

blocks.orig: Also, be wary of pickpockets during the day
blocks.html: Keep an eye out for pickpockets during the day as well

blocks.orig: Only use registered taxi companies if necessary
blocks.html: If you need a taxi, only use registered taxi companies

blocks.orig: The quality of health care in Tanzania varies. In big cities, medical facilities are fair to good, but waiting times are long and prevention is better than cure.
blocks.html: Health care in Tanzania is of varying quality. Medical facilities in the big cities are fair to good, but waiting times are long, and prevention beats cure.

blocks.orig: Getting vaccinations when traveling to Tanzania may be advisable. However, as we are not medically qualified and guidelines may change during the year, we recommend that you consult the health department well in advance of your departure to get the latest information on any vaccinations that may be required for Tanzania.
blocks.html: It may be wise to get vaccinated before travelling to Tanzania. As we are not medically trained and guidelines can change over the year, we advise you to contact the health department well before departure for the latest information on which vaccinations may be required for Tanzania.

blocks.orig: Information regarding the yellow fever vaccine can sometimes be confusing. We’re here to clarify this point for you, when it comes to entry in Tanzania.
blocks.html: Details about the yellow fever vaccine are sometimes confusing. We would like to clear this up for you as far as entry into Tanzania is concerned.

blocks.orig: You do not need a yellow fever vaccination if you are travelling directly from Europe or the United States to Tanzania?
blocks.html: Is a yellow fever vaccination needed if you fly directly from Europe or the United States to Tanzania?

blocks.orig: The government of Tanzania only requires proof of yellow fever vaccination upon arrival if you are traveling from a country with risk of yellow fever (click here to view the list of high-risk countries).
blocks.html: The Tanzanian government only asks for proof of yellow fever vaccination on arrival when you travel from a country where yellow fever is a risk (see the list of high-risk countries here).

blocks.orig: However, if you have a transit in one of the high-risk countries for more than 12 hours, you will be required to get vaccinated. However, we firmly recommend checking with your doctor as he/she will advise you.
blocks.html: If, however, you transit through one of the high-risk countries for more than 12 hours, vaccination becomes compulsory. In any case we strongly advise you to consult your doctor, who can advise you further.

blocks.orig: Should your doctor recommend against the vaccine for one of these reasons, you can still travel to Tanzania from a high risk country with an official letter from the doctor. Showing it to the immigration officer upon arrival would waive the requirement and your trip will go on as planned!
blocks.html: If your doctor advises against the vaccine for one of these reasons, you may still enter Tanzania from a high risk country with an official letter from the doctor. Present it to the immigration officer on arrival and the requirement is waived, so your trip continues as planned!

blocks.orig: According to the World Health Organization’s classification, Tanzania is Yellow fever free.
blocks.html: Under the World Health Organization’s classification, Tanzania counts as Yellow fever free.

blocks.orig: Make sure that all your vaccinations are documented in your vaccination card. If you don’t have one yet, you can get one from your doctor. Don’t forget to take this with you. Customs could ask for this on arrival. In addition, it provides important information in case of a doctor visit. It is also advisable to bring your own first aid kit to Tanzania. This should include plasters, (sterile) gauze, anti-blistering agents, iodine, and medicines for common ailments such as headaches and bowel problems, among other things. It is also good to bring sanitary towels and tampons. These can be difficult to obtain in some areas.
blocks.html: Make sure every vaccination is recorded in your vaccination card. If you don’t have one yet, your doctor can issue one. Don’t forget to pack it, as customs may ask to see it on arrival, and it also gives useful information should you need to see a doctor. We also advise bringing your own first aid kit to Tanzania, containing among other things plasters, (sterile) gauze, blister treatment, iodine and medicines for everyday complaints such as headaches and bowel problems. Sanitary towels and tampons are worth packing too, since they can be hard to find in some areas.

blocks.orig: Casual clothing is worn in Tanzania. It is common practice to cover shoulders and wear skirts and pants that reach below the knees. In Zanzibar, most women cover their hair as well. However, these rules are not very strict. The accommodations you stay in are not subject to strict dress codes. So shorts or skirts are no problem here.
blocks.html: Dress in Tanzania is casual. It is customary to cover your shoulders and to wear skirts and trousers that come below the knee. On Zanzibar most women also cover their hair. These customs are not applied very strictly, however, and the accommodation you stay in has no strict dress code, so shorts and skirts are fine there.

blocks.orig: Tanzania is south of the equator, so the sun can be very strong. Too much sun can lead to dehydration, nausea, dizziness, or headaches. It is therefore good to wear a hat and dark sunglasses during the day. Sunscreen is also a must.
blocks.html: Because Tanzania lies south of the equator, the sun can be fierce. Too much of it may cause dehydration, nausea, dizziness or headaches, so wear a hat and dark sunglasses during the day. Sunscreen is essential as well.

blocks.orig: After sunset it is advisable to wear long trousers (and possibly long sleeves) because of the mosquitoes. Bring a sweater or jacket for the early mornings and cooler evenings, especially in the mountainous regions of Tanzania it gets chilly. We also recommend comfortable (sports) shoes and swimwear for your vacation in Zanzibar and for the lodges with a swimming pool.
blocks.html: Once the sun has set, long trousers (and perhaps long sleeves) are advisable because of the mosquitoes. Pack a jumper or jacket for early mornings and cooler evenings; the mountainous parts of Tanzania in particular get chilly. We also suggest comfortable (sports) shoes, plus swimwear for your stay on Zanzibar and for lodges with a swimming pool.

blocks.orig: During the safari it is common to wear casual clothing, preferably cotton and in safari colors. We do not recommend wearing dark or bright colors (black, blue, red) during the safari – this will attract flies and insects. Colors that don’t stand out, like khaki or olive green, are best.
blocks.html: On safari, casual clothing is the norm, ideally cotton and in safari colours. We advise against dark or bright colours (black, blue, red) while on safari – they attract flies and insects. Shades that don’t stand out, such as khaki or olive green, work best.

blocks.orig: Food and drinks in the lodges, camps and resorts in Tanzania are mostly European style, but with a selection of Tanzanian dishes. There is a full English breakfast with eggs, bacon, tomatoes, cereal and delicious tropical fruits served in the mornings. Lunch often consists of hot meals and dinner is a three or more course meal. In smaller lodges and camps, meals are usually served as a set menu. The larger lodges usually offer lunch and dinner in buffet form. The local beer (the most famous being Kilimanjaro, Serengeti and Safari) is good to drink and there is often a choice of several wines. The tap water is not suitable for consumption. That is why there is a bottle or jug ​​of purified drinking water in the rooms. You can also buy bottled drinking water at each lodge. Make sure you are drinking enough water. The heat in Tanzania can cause you to unconsciously lose a lot of liquids. During the safari you will receive lunch as a packed lunch, which you can enjoy at special picnic areas along the way.
blocks.html: Meals and drinks in the lodges, camps and resorts of Tanzania are mainly European in style, with a choice of Tanzanian dishes alongside. In the morning there is a full English breakfast with eggs, bacon, tomatoes, cereal and delicious tropical fruit. Lunch is often a hot meal and dinner has three or more courses. Smaller lodges and camps generally serve a set menu, while the larger lodges tend to offer lunch and dinner as a buffet. The local beers (Kilimanjaro, Serengeti and Safari are the best known) are good, and there is usually a selection of wines. Tap water is not drinkable, which is why your room has a bottle or jug of purified drinking water; bottled water can also be bought at every lodge. Be sure to drink enough: in the Tanzanian heat you lose a lot of fluid without noticing. On safari days you get a packed lunch to eat at designated picnic spots along the route.

blocks.orig: In Tanzania you pay in the local currency. The local currency is the Tanzanian Shilling, which is available in 1000, 2000, 5000 and 10,000 Tsh banknotes, as well as 50, 100, 200 and 500 Tsh coins.
blocks.html: Payments in Tanzania are made in the local currency, the Tanzanian Shilling. It comes in banknotes of 1000, 2000, 5000 and 10,000 Tsh and in coins of 50, 100, 200 and 500 Tsh.

blocks.orig: The Tanzanian shilling is not available and tradable outside of Tanzania. It is therefore best to bring cash (banknotes) in Euro or US dollars (banknotes from 2006). It’s also nice to bring some change so you can tip the staff if you wish. The best way to change money is when you arrive at the airport.
blocks.html: Outside Tanzania the Tanzanian shilling cannot be bought or exchanged, so it’s best to bring cash (banknotes) in Euro or US dollars (banknotes from 2006). Some small change is handy too, in case you want to tip staff. The airport on arrival is the best place to exchange money.

blocks.orig: You can find ATMs at international airports as well as in the larger villages and in the city. Unfortunately, they don’t always work, so it is good to plan ahead.
blocks.html: ATMs are available at the international airports and in the bigger villages and the city. They don’t always work, unfortunately, so plan ahead.

blocks.orig: Credit cards can also be used. Mastercard is accepted everywhere, Visa and American Express not in all places. In the lodges you can pay with Euros, US-Dollars or credit card and also exchange US-Dollar or Euro for Tanzanian shilling at an (usually) average exchange rate. In the camps, it can be difficult to pay by credit card sometimes due to the remote location and poor connections.
blocks.html: Credit cards are accepted too. Mastercard works everywhere, whereas Visa and American Express are not taken in all places. Lodges accept Euros, US-Dollars or credit card, and will also exchange US-Dollar or Euro for Tanzanian shilling at a (generally) average rate. In the camps, paying by credit card can occasionally be a problem because of the remote location and poor connections.

blocks.orig: Tipping is not mandatory in Tanzania. However, the wages in Tanzania are not high and the employees appreciate tips. We recommend that you only tip if you are satisfied with the service. This often includes small amounts, such as a $ 1 per person tip for those carrying your suitcase to the hotel room. Often it is also possible to give a general tip to the staff when checking out. At the reception there is usually a box specially designed for this purpose.
blocks.html: Tips are not compulsory in Tanzania. Wages are not high, however, and staff are grateful for them. Our advice is to tip only when you are happy with the service. Usually these are small amounts, for instance $ 1 per person for whoever carries your suitcase to your hotel room. On check-out you can often leave a general tip for all staff as well; reception normally has a box set aside for this.

blocks.orig: You can tip your private guide at the end of the safari. Of course, tips should always come from the heart and cannot be an obligation. As a general guideline, we advise to give 10 USD per day per person in your group, for the duration of the safari, as the guide is available to you for the entire safari. Our guides earn decent salaries, but these tips are often used as savings for the extended family (and can for example help a cousin finish school).
blocks.html: At the end of the safari you can tip your private guide. Naturally a tip should come from the heart and is never an obligation. As a rule of thumb we suggest 10 USD per day per person in your group for the length of the safari, since the guide is at your disposal the whole time. Our guides are paid decent salaries, but tips are often put aside as savings for the extended family (helping a cousin complete school, for example).

blocks.orig: Many people want to take beautiful nature photos during a game drive. In this case, it is good to keep a few things in mind:
blocks.html: Many travellers hope to capture beautiful nature shots during a game drive. If that includes you, bear the following in mind:

blocks.orig: Bring enough memory cards and extra batteries. These are not or hardly available in Tanzania
blocks.html: Pack plenty of memory cards and spare batteries, as these are scarce or unavailable in Tanzania

blocks.orig: Bring lens caps, cleaning cloths, and a tight-fitting camera bag to protect the camera from dust
blocks.html: Take lens caps, cleaning cloths and a close-fitting camera bag to keep dust off your camera

blocks.orig: Bring a UV or light filter for the highlands and to protect the lens
blocks.html: A UV or light filter is useful in the highlands and protects the lens

blocks.orig: A zoom lens (e.g. 300 mm) is recommended for photographing wild animals
blocks.html: For photographing wildlife, a zoom lens (300 mm, for example) is advisable

blocks.orig: When charging batteries, note that some tent camps are only powered by a generator for a few hours a day and the voltage fluctuates
blocks.html: Bear in mind when charging batteries that some tented camps only run a generator for a few hours a day, and the voltage is not stable

blocks.orig: When taking pictures of locals, always ask for permission. Nowadays people are more used to cameras, but not everyone likes them. Seeking permission shows respect!
blocks.html: Always ask before photographing local people. Cameras are more familiar these days, yet not everyone appreciates them. Asking first is a sign of respect!

blocks.orig: With a cell phone, you have coverage in many places, but there are places where there isn’t. The lodges and camps in the national parks usually always have a hand radio. They can therefore be reached in an emergency, but this connection is not intended for long phone calls home. Tanzania’s country code is +255.
blocks.html: Mobile phone coverage is available in many places, though there are spots where there isn’t any. Lodges and camps inside the national parks nearly always have a hand radio, so they can be reached in an emergency, but that link is not meant for long calls home. Tanzania’s country code is +255.

blocks.orig: The voltage in Tanzania is not the same as in Europe. The hotels in Tanzania have a voltage of 220-240 volts, which can, however, fluctuate. The sockets are three-pin (English). It is recommended to bring an adapter. Please note that electricity in many lodges and camps is not available 24/7.
blocks.html: Voltage in Tanzania differs from Europe. Hotels run on 220-240 volts, though this can fluctuate. Sockets are of the three-pin (English) type, so bringing an adapter is advisable. Note that in many lodges and camps electricity is not available around the clock.

blocks.orig: We recommend to our customers to get a good travel insurance. A travel insurance often not only covers medical expenses, but also damage or loss of luggage.
blocks.html: We advise all our customers to take out good travel insurance. Besides medical costs, travel insurance usually also covers damaged or lost luggage.

blocks.orig: We also recommend that you get a travel cancellation insurance. Sometimes insurances will only reimburse you up to a certain amount in the event of cancellation – you should check this carefully!
blocks.html: Cancellation insurance is something we recommend as well. Some policies only pay out up to a certain sum if you cancel – do check this carefully!

blocks.orig: The AMREF Flying Doctors have been conducting medical evacuation flights in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda since the 1950s. This Flying Doctor Service is the only flying ambulance with its own doctors and pilots that is on standby 24 hours a day. Flying Doctors Insurance is a supplement to your regular travel insurance and is not compulsory. In an emergency, however, they arrange for an immediate evacuation from remote areas to the hospital in Nairobi. The insurance costs 25 € per person for a safari of a maximum of fourteen days in Kenya and Tanzania.
blocks.html: Since the 1950s the AMREF Flying Doctors have flown medical evacuations in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda. This Flying Doctor Service is the only flying ambulance with its own doctors and pilots on standby 24 hours a day. Flying Doctors Insurance is an add-on to your normal travel insurance and is not compulsory, but in an emergency they organise immediate evacuation from remote areas to the hospital in Nairobi. The cover costs 25 € per person for a safari of at most fourteen days in Kenya and Tanzania.
